Reproducing Li, Chen, Guo, Gerfen & Svoboda (2015) from CRCNS alm-1¶

Paper. Li N, Chen T-W, Guo ZV, Gerfen CR, Svoboda K (2015). A motor cortex circuit for motor planning and movement. Nature 519, 51-56. doi:10.1038/nature14178. The claims file (claims/crcns-alm-1/10.1038-nature14178.yaml) was written from the version of record (main text, Methods and the legends of Figures 1 to 5 and Extended Data Figures 1 to 7).

Data set. CRCNS alm-1, "Extracellular recordings from anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM) neurons of adult mice performing a tactile decision behavior", doi:10.6080/K0RF5RZT, read from the public bucket crcnsarchive under alm-1/live/. Version: unversioned. CRCNS data sets have no versions; the bucket holds alm-1/live/ (the data) and alm-1/version_1/ and alm-1/version_2/, which hold only earlier copies of the documentation, and alm-1/live/old/, three example sessions that the data description says are superseded. The paper cites no version, so the only published copy of the data, live, is used. A later change can be detected with the MD5 sums of the files read, from the data set's checksums.md5 (checked against the bucket below):

The session files (MATLAB "data structure" files, one tar.gz per animal) are used. The same sessions are also in NWB 1.0 files, which lack the photostimulation type, the AOM and laser power traces and the GoodTrials flag, so they are not used. The raw voltage traces (about 800 GB) are not read. The data set also holds the authors' MATLAB scripts that "reproduce the figures" and their compiled output (ALM_compiled_all_data.mat); the output is not read. The scripts are cited below where the paper leaves a detail open.

What the data set holds. The electrophysiology of Figures 2 and 3 and Extended Data Figures 1, 2 and 5: 99 sessions from 19 mice, 1,408 units with cell type labels, trial types, epoch times, photostimulation type per trial, and the lick, AOM and laser power traces. The photoinhibition and photoactivation behaviour (Figs 1 and 5, ED Figs 3 and 6), the imaging (Fig. 4), the anatomy (ED Fig. 3) and the recordings with somatic PT photoactivation (ED Fig. 7) are not in it.

Lick right trials are contralateral to the recorded left ALM. "R" and "L" below are lick right and lick left trials. Loading streams about 14 GB and takes about four minutes.

import time
import warnings
from collections import Counter

import fsspec
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

import alm

pd.set_option("display.width", 200)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 40)
pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 200)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)

started = time.time()
S = alm.load_all(workers=4)
meta = alm.load_meta()
print(f"{alm.DATASET} ({alm.VERSION}, doi:{alm.DATASET_DOI}): {len(S)} sessions streamed in {time.time() - started:.0f} s")

with fsspec.open(alm.BASE + "checksums.md5", "rt") as fh:
    md5 = dict(line.split()[::-1] for line in fh if line.strip())
read = ["datafiles/meta_data_files.tar.gz"] + [f"datafiles/data_structure_files/data_structure_{a}.tar.gz" for a in alm.ANIMALS]
print("MD5 sums on the bucket now (compare with the header):")
for f in read:
    print(f"  {md5.get(f)}  {f}")

T = pd.concat([s["trials"] for s in S], ignore_index=True)
units = [(s, u) for s in S for u in s["units"]]
meta["animal"] = meta.session.str[:9]
geno = meta.groupby("animal").agg(strain=("strain", "first"), gene=("gene", "first"), sessions=("session", "size"),
                                  photostim_location=("photostim_location", "first"))
per_animal = pd.DataFrame({
    "sessions": pd.Series(Counter(s["animal"] for s in S)),
    "units": pd.Series(Counter(s["animal"] for s, u in units)),
    "trials": T.groupby("animal").size()})
print(per_animal.join(geno[["strain", "gene", "photostim_location"]]).to_string())
print(f"\nAnimals {len(per_animal)}, sessions {len(S)}, units {len(units)} (data description: 19 animals, 99 sessions, 1,408 units)")
print("Meta data files:", len(meta), "; sessions with a meta data file:", len(set(meta.session) & {s['session'] for s in S}))
print("Strains (paper, Methods: 9 Sim1_KJ18-Cre, 3 Rbp4-Cre, 4 Tlx_PL56-Cre injected; 1 Sim1 x Ai32, 2 Tlx x Ai32):")
print(geno.groupby(["strain", "gene"]).size().to_string())

cite = {"matlab_scripts/analyses_scripts/analysis_compile_all_data.m": [(124, 127), (132, 137), (217, 221), (299, 300), (352, 352), (485, 485)],
        "matlab_scripts/analyses_scripts/analysis_ALM_IT_PT_selectivity.m": [(25, 25), (170, 170), (195, 195)],
        "matlab_scripts/analyses_scripts/analysis_ALM_error_trial_selectivity.m": [(99, 100)],
        "matlab_scripts/demos/Demo_get_performance.m": [(70, 73)]}
for f, spans in cite.items():
    with fsspec.open(alm.BASE + f, "rt", encoding="latin-1") as fh:
        lines = fh.read().splitlines()
    print(f"== {f}")
    for a, b in spans:
        for i in range(a, b + 1):
            print(f"{i:4d}: {lines[i - 1].strip()[:150]}")

# Trials of type NaN ("do not analyse") that carry light, by mouse and session: when the light
# starts relative to the epochs, pulse count and width, and power.
nanl = T[T.ptype.isna() & T.has_light].copy()
nanl["onset_epoch"] = np.select([nanl.cue.isna(), nanl.stim_on < nanl.pole_in, nanl.stim_on < nanl.pole_out, nanl.stim_on < nanl.cue],
                                ["no cue (not performing)", "pre-sample", "sample", "delay"], "response or later")
print("NaN-type trials:", int(T.ptype.isna().sum()), "; with light:", len(nanl))
print(nanl.groupby(["animal", "session"]).agg(trials=("stim_on", "size"), onset_s_min=("stim_on", "min"),
      onset_s_median=("stim_on", "median"), onset_s_max=("stim_on", "max"), pulses=("n_pulses", "median"),
      pulse_ms=("pulse_ms", "median"), power_mW=("power_max", "median"),
      performing=("good", "sum")).round(2).to_string())
print("\nOnset epoch of the light in NaN-type trials, by mouse:")
print(pd.crosstab(nanl.animal, nanl.onset_epoch).to_string())
print("\nStrain of the mice with NaN-type light trials:", geno.loc[sorted(nanl.animal.unique()), "strain"].to_dict())

samp = nanl[nanl.onset_epoch == "sample"]

print(samp.assign(pulse_ms=samp.pulse_ms.round(1), power_mW=samp.power_max.round(0))
      .groupby(["animal", "n_pulses", "pulse_ms", "power_mW"]).size().rename("trials").to_string())

Two things in the trial tables are not in the description. Photostimulation types 3, 4 and 5 occur in the two Tlx_PL56-Cre x Ai32 mice: eight 1 ms pulses at about 23 mW starting 1.8, 2.3 or 2.8 s into the trial (table by mouse above); the description lists only 0, 1, 2 and NaN. The authors' compile script counts types 1 to 5 as tagging trials. And in one session of ANM210862, 43 trials of type 0 ("non-stimulation") carry 50 ms light pulses at 47.1 mW starting 1.9 to 4.35 s into the trial (above). Trials of type 0 with light are kept as the data label them, as the paper's analysis would have; how many enter is printed. The NaN-type trials ("photostimulation configurations for testing purposes, these trials should not be analyze", data description) carry light in 3,756 trials of all 19 mice. Light starting in the sample epoch occurs in 367 of them: 347 in the two Tlx_PL56-Cre x Ai32 mice (IT neurons) and the one Sim1_KJ18-Cre x Ai32 mouse ANM218693 (3 sessions, 59 units), as eight 1 ms pulses, at about 23 mW in all but 2 (47 mW), and 20 in five other mice (table above). None of this matches the sample-epoch PT photostimulation of ED Fig. 7 (two mice, eight sessions, 91 neurons), and the NaN-type trials are left out everywhere. The epoch lengths fit the Methods' 1.3 s sample and delay epochs.

In 3,707 of 28,465 performing trials the sample or delay epoch differs from 1.3 s by more than 50 ms (1,859 of them correct trials without stimulation); epoch rates divide by each trial's own epoch length, so these trials are kept. 10 units, 7 of them from one session, have spike times out of order; every measure here bins or sorts spikes, so this does not change them.

The labels give 1,173 pyramidal, 45 pyramidal and PT, 27 pyramidal and IT, 124 FS and 39 units without a label: 1,245 pyramidal in all, as the paper says. Waveforms are sampled every 0.0512 ms, so trough-to-peak widths come in steps of that size; the claim on unit counts compares both the labels and widths recomputed from the waveforms.

Clocks. Three checks show the streams share the trial clock. Spikes and trial times: the number of pyramidal neurons that distinguish lick right from lick left trials, in 200 ms windows, is near the 5% expected by chance before the sample epoch and rises after it (claim fig2c-selectivity-time-course, printed there with the same count when the trial labels are shuffled). Spikes and the AOM trace: antidromic spikes follow the light pulses at a fixed latency, with a jitter near 0.1 ms (claim antidromic-latency-jitter). Lick trace and cue: an onset of the lick trace is found in the 1 s after the cue in 96.6% of correct trials, and in 90% of those it falls 34 to 173 ms after the cue (printed next; example traces under reaction-time). The lick counts printed next cross a fixed 1 V, although session baselines run from 0.07 to 4.83 V; they serve only as this clock check.

task-performance¶

Mice performed the task at 78.4% correct on average, with responses before the go cue on fewer than 13% of trials (n = 42 mice).

Only the 19 electrophysiology mice are in the data set, against 42 in the paper. Per cent correct is hits over hits and errors, lick early trials excluded (Methods); no-lick trials are left out, as the data set's Demo_get_performance.m does. Lick early fraction is over all performing trials of the same set. Readings from the criterion: mean over sessions (a), over mice (b), pooled trials (c); control trials (type 0, no StimTrials flag) or all performing trials except the NaN-type test trials, which the data description says are not to be analysed.

rows = []
for trials_name, sel in (("control", (T.ptype == 0) & ~T.StimTrials), ("all but NaN-type", T.ptype.notna())):
    d = T[(T.good == 1) & sel & T.cue.notna()]
    d = d.assign(hit=d.HitR | d.HitL, resp=d.HitR | d.HitL | d.ErrR | d.ErrL)
    ne = d[~d.LickEarly & d.resp]
    ps = ne.groupby("session").hit.mean() * 100
    le_s = d.groupby("session").LickEarly.mean() * 100
    pm = ne.groupby("animal").hit.mean() * 100
    le_m = d.groupby("animal").LickEarly.mean() * 100
    for how, pc, le in (("a sessions", ps.mean(), le_s.mean()), ("b mice", ne.assign(s=ne.session).groupby("animal").apply(lambda x: x.groupby("session").hit.mean().mean()).mean() * 100, d.groupby("animal").apply(lambda x: x.groupby("session").LickEarly.mean().mean()).mean() * 100),
                        ("c pooled", ne.hit.mean() * 100, d.LickEarly.mean() * 100)):
        rows.append({"trials": trials_name, "mean": how, "per_cent_correct": pc, "lick_early_pct": le,
                     "within_tolerance": abs(pc - 78.4) <= 7.84, "lick_early_below_14.3": le < 14.3, "n_trials": len(d)})
perf = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(perf.round(2).to_string(index=False))

unit-counts¶

1,408 single units were recorded in left ALM from 19 mice in 99 sessions; by spike width, 1,245 are putative pyramidal neurons (> 0.45 ms), 124 fast-spiking neurons (< 0.35 ms) and 39 intermediate units excluded.

# variant: the width on a waveform interpolated to 1 us (cubic spline)
from scipy.interpolate import CubicSpline
def width_interp(wf):
    x = np.arange(len(wf)) / alm.FS_WAVEFORM * 1e3
    xs = np.arange(0, x[-1], 0.001)
    ys = CubicSpline(x, wf)(xs)
    i = int(np.argmin(ys)); j = i + int(np.argmax(ys[i:]))
    return xs[j] - xs[i]

Result: partially reproduced. The data set holds 1,408 units from 19 mice in 99 sessions, and its cell type labels give exactly 1,245 pyramidal, 124 FS and 39 unclassified units. Recomputed as the criterion says, from the trough-to-peak interval of the deposited mean waveforms, 1,245 units are above 0.45 ms, as the paper has, but 158 are below 0.35 ms and 5 in between, against 124 and 39: 34 of the 39 unlabelled units have widths below 0.35 ms. The spline-interpolated variant gives 1,241, 158 and 9. The waveform arrays are read the right way round (29 samples per spike, one row per spike for all 1,408 units, trough at sample 15 in every unit). The labels are a clean function of the deposited width: every FS unit measures 0.154 to 0.256 ms, every unlabelled unit 0.307 (34) or 0.410 ms (5), every pyramidal unit 0.461 to 0.666 ms, so the labels put the FS boundary between 0.256 and 0.307 ms (5 and 6 samples), not at the Methods' 0.35 ms. The unlabelled units' waveforms are as small as the FS units' (median trough 120 against 132 µV; pyramidal 204 µV). How the paper's widths map onto these samples is not stated; the labels hold its classification, the stated thresholds applied to the deposited waveforms do not.

fig2-selective-fraction¶

73% (912 of 1,245) of putative pyramidal neurons distinguish the trial types in at least one epoch.

Two-tailed t-test (pooled variance) of spike rates on lick right against lick left correct trials, in the sample, delay or response epoch, P < 0.05 uncorrected (Methods). Under each reading of the response epoch and of lick early trials. The test is on rates, as the data set's compile script runs it (lines 217 to 221 and 300, printed in the data check); the Methods say spike counts, which differ from rates where an epoch is not 1.3 s, so a test on counts and Welch's test are variants.

Result: reproduced. With lick early trials dropped and a 1.3 s response epoch, 912 of 1,245 pyramidal neurons (73.25%) are selective, the paper's numbers exactly. The other readings give 910 to 950 (73.1% to 76.3%) and Welch's test 903 to 947. The t-test on spike counts, the Methods' wording, gives 912 again under the main readings and 910 to 944 under the others (the data set's compile script tests rates, lines 217 to 221 and 300 printed above). All are within tolerance. Per mouse the fraction ranges from 0.417 to 0.852.

fig2c-selectivity-time-course¶

Selectivity emerges in the sample epoch, increases through the delay epoch and is largest at the beginning of the response epoch.

Measure 1 (ED Fig. 1f): the number of pyramidal neurons significant (two-tailed t-test on spike counts, P < 0.05) in 200 ms windows, stepped by 10 ms. Measure 2 (Fig. 2c): the population selectivity of the selective neurons, preferred minus non-preferred rate, with the preference set from 10 random trials of each type (by spike count from sample onset to the end of the response epoch, as the data set's compile script does) and the rate difference taken on the remaining trials. Neurons need at least 11 trials of each type for the split; the data set's script requires more than 15, a variant. The epoch boundaries relative to the cue are the medians over trials. Seeds are fixed.

In [14]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(20150305)
t_sample = -float(np.median(g.cue - g.pole_in))
t_delay = -float(np.median(g.cue - g.pole_out))
print(f"Median sample onset {t_sample:.3f} s and delay onset {t_delay:.3f} s relative to the cue")
cnt_sig, cnt_sig_shuf, popsel, popsel15, n_pop = None, None, [], [], 0
sel_keys = set(map(tuple, pyr[pyr.selective][["session", "unit"]].values))
pyr_keys = set(map(tuple, pyr[["session", "unit"]].values))
for s, u in units:
    key = (s["session"], u["unit"])
    if key not in pyr_keys:
        continue
    tr = s["trials"]
    r, l = alm.trial_mask(tr, u)
    if r.sum() < 2 or l.sum() < 2:
        continue
    br, bl = alm.cue_binned(u, tr, r), alm.cue_binned(u, tr, l)
    wr, centers = alm.window_sums(br)
    wl, _ = alm.window_sums(bl)
    p = stats.ttest_ind(wr, wl, axis=0).pvalue
    p = np.where(np.isnan(p), 1, p)
    allw = np.vstack([wr, wl])
    perm = rng.permutation(len(allw))
    ps = stats.ttest_ind(allw[perm[:len(wr)]], allw[perm[len(wr):]], axis=0).pvalue
    ps = np.where(np.isnan(ps), 1, ps)
    cnt_sig = (p < 0.05).astype(int) if cnt_sig is None else cnt_sig + (p < 0.05)
    cnt_sig_shuf = (ps < 0.05).astype(int) if cnt_sig_shuf is None else cnt_sig_shuf + (ps < 0.05)
    if key in sel_keys and r.sum() >= 11 and l.sum() >= 11:
        ir, il = rng.permutation(r.sum()), rng.permutation(l.sum())
        whole = lambda b: b[:, (alm.CUE_EDGES[:-1] >= t_sample) & (alm.CUE_EDGES[:-1] < alm.RESPONSE_S)].sum(axis=1)
        pref_r = whole(br)[ir[:10]].mean() >= whole(bl)[il[:10]].mean()
        diff = (wr[ir[10:]].mean(axis=0) - wl[il[10:]].mean(axis=0)) / alm.WIN_S
        popsel.append(diff if pref_r else -diff)
        if r.sum() > 15 and l.sum() > 15:
            popsel15.append(popsel[-1])
popsel, popsel15 = np.array(popsel), np.array(popsel15)
print("Neurons in measure 1:", None if cnt_sig is None else "pyramidal with >= 2 trials of each type",
      "; in measure 2:", len(popsel), "(>15 trials each:", len(popsel15), ")")

def at(x, t):
    return float(x[np.argmin(np.abs(centers - t))])

def check(x, name):
    rng_t = (centers >= -3.4) & (centers <= 1.9)
    tmax = float(centers[rng_t][np.argmax(x[rng_t])])
    v = {"measure": name, "pre_sample": at(x, t_sample - 0.1), "sample_end": at(x, t_delay - 0.1),
         "delay_start": at(x, t_delay + 0.1), "delay_end": at(x, -0.1), "max_value": float(x[rng_t].max()), "t_max_s": tmax}
    v["emerges"] = v["sample_end"] > v["pre_sample"]
    v["increases_in_delay"] = v["delay_end"] > v["delay_start"]
    v["max_within_0.5s"] = 0 < tmax <= 0.5
    v["max_within_0.2s"] = 0 < tmax <= 0.2
    return v

res = pd.DataFrame([check(cnt_sig.astype(float), "1 significant neurons"), check(popsel.mean(axis=0), "2 population selectivity"),
                    check(popsel15.mean(axis=0), "2 variant, >15 trials")])
print(res.round(3).to_string(index=False))
print("\nShuffled labels, significant neurons: median", int(np.median(cnt_sig_shuf)), "max", int(cnt_sig_shuf.max()),
      "; true labels before sample onset (window centred 0.1 s before):", int(at(cnt_sig, t_sample - 0.1)),
      "; 5% of the neurons tested:", round(0.05 * len(pyr)))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.2))
ax[0].plot(centers, cnt_sig, "k"); ax[0].plot(centers, cnt_sig_shuf, color="0.6")
ax[1].plot(centers, popsel.mean(axis=0), "k")
for a in ax:
    for x in (t_sample, t_delay, 0):
        a.axvline(x, color="0.7", ls=":")
    a.set_xlabel("time from cue (s)")
ax[0].set_ylabel("significant neurons"); ax[1].set_ylabel("pref - nonpref (spikes/s)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("Plotted ranges: significant neurons", int(cnt_sig.min()), "to", int(cnt_sig.max()), "; population selectivity",
      round(float(popsel.mean(axis=0).min()), 2), "to", round(float(popsel.mean(axis=0).max()), 2), "spikes/s")

Both measures meet all three conditions under both readings (maximum within 0.2 s of the cue).

fig2c-dynamic-single-neurons¶

Individual neuron responses are dynamic while selectivity at the population level is stable.

Population response correlation (Methods): for the selective neurons, each neuron's cue-aligned rate (200 ms window, 10 ms step, correct trials) is mean-subtracted and divided by the variance of its response across the trial (as the Methods say; the data set's script does the same; division by the s.d. is a variant). Pearson's r between the population vector at each time and at the cue. Readings (a) the vector of selectivities (R minus L) and (b) the R and L rates concatenated. The population selectivity is measure 2 of the previous claim.

In [15]:
PR, PL = [], []
for s, u in units:
    if (s["session"], u["unit"]) not in sel_keys:
        continue
    tr = s["trials"]
    r, l = alm.trial_mask(tr, u)
    if r.sum() < 2 or l.sum() < 2:
        continue
    PR.append(alm.window_sums(alm.cue_binned(u, tr, r))[0].mean(axis=0) / alm.WIN_S)
    PL.append(alm.window_sums(alm.cue_binned(u, tr, l))[0].mean(axis=0) / alm.WIN_S)
PR, PL = np.array(PR), np.array(PL)
span = (centers >= -3.4) & (centers <= 1.9)
def norm(x, how):
    x = x[:, span]
    x = x - x.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    d = x.var(axis=1, keepdims=True) if how == "var" else x.std(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return x / np.where(d == 0, np.nan, d)
cs = centers[span]
i0 = np.argmin(np.abs(cs))
win_early = (cs >= t_sample) & (cs <= t_delay + 0.5)
rows, curves = [], {}
for how in ("var", "sd"):
    nr, nl = norm(PR, how), norm(PL, how)
    for reading, M in (("a selectivity", nr - nl), ("b concatenated", np.vstack([nr, nl]))):
        ok = ~np.isnan(M).any(axis=1)
        M = M[ok]
        rc = np.array([np.corrcoef(M[:, j], M[:, i0])[0, 1] for j in range(M.shape[1])])
        curves[(how, reading)] = rc
        rows.append({"normalised_by": how, "reading": reading, "neurons_rows": int(ok.sum()),
                     "mean_r_sample_to_delay+0.5": rc[win_early].mean(), "max_r_in_that_window": rc[win_early].max(),
                     "r_at_delay_end_-0.1s": rc[np.argmin(np.abs(cs + 0.1))]})
dyn = pd.DataFrame(rows)
dyn["below_0.5"] = dyn["mean_r_sample_to_delay+0.5"] < 0.5
print(dyn.round(3).to_string(index=False))
ps_curve = popsel.mean(axis=0)
stable = (centers >= t_delay - 0.1) & (centers <= -0.1)
print("\nPopulation selectivity from the end of the sample epoch through the delay: min", round(float(ps_curve[stable].min()), 3),
      "spikes/s; all above 0:", bool((ps_curve[stable] > 0).all()))

normalised_by        reading  neurons_rows  mean_r_sample_to_delay+0.5  max_r_in_that_window  r_at_delay_end_-0.1s  below_0.5
          var  a selectivity           912                      -0.168                -0.024                 0.279       True
          var b concatenated          1824                      -0.159                -0.042                 0.349       True
           sd  a selectivity           912                      -0.041                 0.239                 0.737       True
           sd b concatenated          1824                      -0.084                 0.254                 0.720       True

Result: reproduced, resting on the claims file's 0.5 bound. The mean population response correlation with the cue-time vector over the sample epoch and the first 0.5 s of the delay is -0.168 (reading a) and -0.159 (reading b), with maxima of -0.024 and -0.042 in that span; with division by the s.d. it is -0.041 and -0.084. All are below 0.5, while the population selectivity stays above 0 from the end of the sample epoch through the delay (minimum 1.19 spikes/s).

ed2-error-trials-predict-choice¶

On error trials, when mice lick opposite to the instructed direction, ALM activity predicts the licking direction; most selective neurons switch their trial type preference.

Error trials are labelled by the instructed side (ErrR: pole for lick right, mouse licked left). Per selective pyramidal neuron and epoch, correct selectivity R minus L and error selectivity ErrR minus ErrL. Readings: at least 1 or at least 5 error trials of each type; the data set's script uses more than 10 correct and more than 5 error trials of each type (variant).

In [16]:
rows = []
sp = pyr[pyr.selective]
for name, m in (("min 1 error each", (sp.n_errR >= 1) & (sp.n_errL >= 1)), ("min 5 error each", (sp.n_errR >= 5) & (sp.n_errL >= 5)),
                ("script: >10 correct, >5 error", (sp.n_R > 10) & (sp.n_L > 10) & (sp.n_errR > 5) & (sp.n_errL > 5))):
    d = sp[m]
    for e in ("sample", "delay", "response"):
        c = d[f"{e}_R"] - d[f"{e}_L"]
        er = d[f"{e}_errR"] - d[f"{e}_errL"]
        r, p = stats.pearsonr(c, er)
        nz = (c != 0) & (er != 0)
        rows.append({"reading": name, "epoch": e, "neurons": len(d), "r": r, "p": p,
                     "fraction_switched": float((np.sign(c[nz]) != np.sign(er[nz])).mean()), "n_nonzero": int(nz.sum())})
err = pd.DataFrame(rows)
err["holds"] = (err.r < 0) & (err.p < 0.05) & (err.fraction_switched > 0.5)
print(err.round(4).to_string(index=False))
print("\nSelective pyramidal neurons without error trials of both types:", int(((sp.n_errR < 1) | (sp.n_errL < 1)).sum()), "of", len(sp))
print("\nUnder the four readings of the shared methods (selection 'min 1 error each'):")
rows = []
for (le, resp), d in UT.items():
    sp_ = d[(d.label == "pyramidal") & d.selective & (d.n_errR >= 1) & (d.n_errL >= 1)]
    for e in ("sample", "delay", "response"):
        c, er = sp_[f"{e}_R"] - sp_[f"{e}_L"], sp_[f"{e}_errR"] - sp_[f"{e}_errL"]
        nz = (c != 0) & (er != 0)
        r, p = stats.pearsonr(c, er)
        rows.append({"lick_early": le, "response_s": resp, "epoch": e, "neurons": len(sp_), "r": r, "p": p,
                     "fraction_switched": float((np.sign(c[nz]) != np.sign(er[nz])).mean())})
er4 = pd.DataFrame(rows)
er4["holds"] = (er4.r < 0) & (er4.p < 0.05) & (er4.fraction_switched > 0.5)
print(er4.round(4).to_string(index=False))

Result: reproduced. Under both readings and the script's selection, correct and error selectivity are negatively correlated in all three epochs (sample r = -0.085 to -0.123, P 0.006 to 0.017; delay r = -0.43 to -0.48; response r = -0.44 to -0.50, printed P < 0.0001), and the fraction of neurons whose error selectivity has the opposite sign exceeds one half in every epoch (0.507 to 0.652). The four readings of the shared methods give the same (sample r = -0.082 to -0.097, P 0.004 to 0.018; switched fractions 0.502 to 0.627). In the sample epoch the correlation is weak and the fraction just above one half (0.502 to 0.507 with at least one error trial of each type).

fig2e-equal-contra-ipsi¶

Among selective putative pyramidal neurons, contra-preferring and ipsi-preferring neurons are present in equal proportions (427 contra-preferring and 485 ipsi-preferring in Fig. 2c).

Preference from the spike rates from sample onset to the end of the response epoch, R against L (reading a, all correct trials; Methods), or from the 10-trial split of the previous claims (reading b). The test is the Methods' bootstrap over neurons, one-tailed, 10^4 resamples.

In [17]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
sp = pyr[pyr.selective]
ca = sp.contra.values
pb = popsel  # sign convention: the 10-trial split's preference is in the sign of R-L on held-out trials below
rows = [{"reading": "a total counts", "contra": int(ca.sum()), "ipsi": int((~ca).sum()), "fraction_contra": ca.mean(),
         "P_more_contra": alm.bootstrap_more_ipsi(ca, rng=rng)}]
# reading b: preference from 10 random trials of each type
rng_b = np.random.default_rng(3)
cb = []
for s, u in units:
    if (s["session"], u["unit"]) not in sel_keys:
        continue
    tr = s["trials"]
    r, l = alm.trial_mask(tr, u)
    if r.sum() < 11 or l.sum() < 11:
        continue
    a, b = alm.epoch_bounds(tr)["trial"]
    cr, cl = alm.counts_in(u, tr, r, a, b), alm.counts_in(u, tr, l, a, b)
    cb.append(cr[rng_b.permutation(len(cr))[:10]].mean() > cl[rng_b.permutation(len(cl))[:10]].mean())
cb = np.array(cb)
rows.append({"reading": "b 10-trial split", "contra": int(cb.sum()), "ipsi": int((~cb).sum()), "fraction_contra": cb.mean(),
             "P_more_contra": alm.bootstrap_more_ipsi(cb, rng=rng)})
pref = pd.DataFrame(rows)
pref["counts_ok"] = (abs(pref.contra - 427) <= 42.7) & (abs(pref.ipsi - 485) <= 48.5)
pref["no_more_contra"] = pref.P_more_contra >= 0.05
print(pref.round(4).to_string(index=False))
print("\nPer mouse, reading a, fraction contra-preferring:", sp.groupby("animal").contra.mean().round(2).to_dict())
print("Binomial test against 0.5 (variant), reading a: p =", round(stats.binomtest(int(ca.sum()), len(ca)).pvalue, 4))

ed1-no-population-contra-bias¶

The overall spike count of the recorded population shows no significant contralateral bias (P = 0.13, two-tailed t-test against 0).

Per neuron, the difference between its mean spike rate on R and L trials from sample onset to the end of the response epoch; two-tailed one-sample t-test against 0. Readings (a) selective pyramidal neurons, (b) all pyramidal neurons, (c) all units.

In [18]:

    x = (d.trial_R - d.trial_L).dropna()
    t_, p_ = stats.ttest_1samp(x, 0)
    rows.append({"reading": name, "neurons": len(x), "mean_R_minus_L_spk_s": x.mean(), "median": x.median(), "t": t_, "p": p_})
bias = pd.DataFrame(rows)
bias["significant"] = bias.p < 0.05

    print("Variant", le_resp, "all pyramidal: mean", round(x.mean(), 3), "p", round(stats.ttest_1samp(x, 0).pvalue, 4))

ed1-fast-spiking-properties¶

Fast-spiking neurons have higher baseline firing rates and are less selective than putative pyramidal neurons.

Baseline readings: (a) the rate before sample onset (from the start of the trial), (b) the 0.5 s before sample onset; the average of the R and L trial means. Selectivity readings: (a) the fraction selective by the shared test, (b) the absolute rate difference over the three epochs.

In [19]:
fs = D[D.label == "FS"]
rows = []
for name, col in (("a whole pre-sample", "pre_all"), ("b 0.5 s pre-sample", "pre")):
    bf, bp = (fs[f"{col}_R"] + fs[f"{col}_L"]) / 2, (pyr[f"{col}_R"] + pyr[f"{col}_L"]) / 2
    rows.append({"measure": "baseline " + name, "FS_mean": bf.mean(), "pyr_mean": bp.mean(), "FS_median": bf.median(),
                 "pyr_median": bp.median(), "FS_higher": bf.mean() > bp.mean() and bf.median() > bp.median(),
                 "ranksum_p": stats.mannwhitneyu(bf.dropna(), bp.dropna()).pvalue})
rows.append({"measure": "selectivity a fraction selective", "FS_mean": fs.selective.mean(), "pyr_mean": pyr.selective.mean(),
             "FS_less_selective": fs.selective.mean() < pyr.selective.mean()})

Result: partially reproduced. FS neurons have higher baseline rates than pyramidal neurons under both readings (mean 9.03 against 3.97 spikes/s, median 6.40 against 2.37, rank-sum p printed as 0.0). They are not less selective under either of the criterion's readings: 79.8% of FS neurons are selective against 73.3% of pyramidal neurons, and their mean absolute rate difference is larger (2.29 against 1.53 spikes/s). The four readings of the shared methods give the same (FS 79.8% to 84.7% selective against 73.1% to 76.3%; 2.25 to 2.29 against 1.48 to 1.53 spikes/s). Only relative to their rate (a variant the criterion does not name) are FS neurons less selective (median 0.21 against 0.33). The baseline half of the claim holds and the selectivity half does not.

Result: reproduced for the PT and IT counts. The labels give 45 PT neurons in 8 mice and 27 IT neurons in 7 mice, the paper's numbers. The pyramidal-tract-activated and intratelencephalic-activated neurons and the untestable ones have no label, so those counts cannot be reported.

The data set labels only the neurons that passed the collision test. The pyramidal-tract- and intratelencephalic-activated neurons (22 and 106) and the 7 that could not be tested carry no label, so their counts cannot be read from the data set.

antidromic-latency-jitter¶

PT neurons have shorter antidromic latencies than IT neurons (mean 2.7 against 4.6 ms) and both have small jitter (mean s.d. 0.1 and 0.2 ms) ...; the mean jitter of tagged neurons is 0.15 ms.

Pulse onsets are read from the AOM input trace (10 kHz, so 0.1 ms steps); spike times are at the 19531.25 Hz sampling of the recording. For each PT neuron, the PT axonal stimulation trials (type 1); for each IT neuron, the IT trials (type 2, and in a variant also the undocumented types 3 to 5). Latency is the first spike within 10 ms of a pulse onset (before the second pulse). The paper does not say how antidromic spikes are told from spontaneous ones; here they are the spikes within ±1 ms of the neuron's modal latency (0.2 ms bins), with ±0.5 ms and a robust s.d. (1.4826 times the median absolute deviation within ±1 ms) as variants (an assumption). The second cell counts, per neuron, the spikes observed between 0.5 and 1 ms from the mode against those expected from the spontaneous background, and draws the latency histograms of the IT neurons with both windows marked. The third gives readings that need no window: a per-neuron fit of a Gaussian peak plus a uniform background, the same with a broad Gaussian added for broad stimulus-locked humps, and the ±1 ms jitter without the four IT neurons whose histograms show such humps. Readings: (a) first pulse of each pair, (b) both pulses pooled.

def lat_table(it_types, hw):
    rows = []
    for s, u in units:
        tag = "PT" if "PT" in u["cell_types"] else "IT" if "IT" in u["cell_types"] else ""
        if not tag:
            continue
        types = {1.0} if tag == "PT" else it_types
        l0 = alm.antidromic_latencies(s, u, types, order=0)
        l1 = alm.antidromic_latencies(s, u, types, order=1)
        for reading, lat in (("a first pulse", l0), ("b both pulses", np.r_[l0, l1])):
            m, sd, n, nr = alm.latency_mode_stats(lat, hw)
            rows.append({"session": s["session"], "unit": u["unit"], "animal": s["animal"], "tag": tag, "reading": reading,
                         "latency_ms": m, "jitter_ms": sd, "n_resp": n, "n_pulses": len(lat), "p_resp": n / max(len(lat), 1)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

LT = {}
summ = []
for it_types, it_name in (({2.0}, "IT type 2"), ({2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0}, "IT types 2-5")):
    for hw in (1.0, 0.5):
        lt = lat_table(it_types, hw)
        LT[(it_name, hw)] = lt
        for reading, d in lt.groupby("reading"):
            ok = d[d.n_resp >= 3]
            pt, it = ok[ok.tag == "PT"], ok[ok.tag == "IT"]
            summ.append({"IT trials": it_name, "window_ms": hw, "reading": reading, "PT_n": len(pt), "IT_n": len(it),
                         "PT_latency": pt.latency_ms.mean(), "IT_latency": it.latency_ms.mean(),
                         "PT_jitter": pt.jitter_ms.mean(), "IT_jitter": it.jitter_ms.mean(), "tagged_jitter": ok.jitter_ms.mean(),
                         "PT_latency_median": pt.latency_ms.median(), "IT_latency_median": it.latency_ms.median()})
lat = pd.DataFrame(summ)
lat["PT_ok"] = (abs(lat.PT_latency - 2.7) <= 0.27) & (abs(lat.PT_jitter - 0.1) <= 0.05)
lat["IT_ok"] = (abs(lat.IT_latency - 4.6) <= 0.46) & (abs(lat.IT_jitter - 0.2) <= 0.05)
lat["tagged_jitter_ok"] = abs(lat.tagged_jitter - 0.15) <= 0.015
lat["PT_shorter"] = lat.PT_latency < lat.IT_latency
print(lat.round(3).to_string(index=False))
main_lt = LT[("IT type 2", 1.0)]
print("\nPer neuron (IT type 2, ±1 ms, first pulse):")
print(main_lt[main_lt.reading == "a first pulse"].round(3).to_string(index=False))

# Which window fits: for each tagged neuron (first pulses; IT type 2 trials), the first-spike
# latencies far from the mode (more than 2 ms) give the spontaneous background, and so the
# number of spikes expected by chance within ±0.5 and ±1 ms of the mode, against those observed.
# The spikes between 0.5 and 1 ms from the mode are antidromic when they far exceed chance.
# A robust jitter (1.4826 x median absolute deviation, within ±1 ms) is a third reading.
rows = []
for s, u in units:
    tag = "PT" if "PT" in u["cell_types"] else "IT" if "IT" in u["cell_types"] else ""
    if not tag:
        continue
    lat = alm.antidromic_latencies(s, u, {1.0} if tag == "PT" else {2.0}, order=0)
    f = lat[np.isfinite(lat)]
    if len(f) < 3:
        continue
    mode = alm.latency_mode(f)
    e05, o05 = alm.latency_background(f, mode, 0.5)
    e10, o10 = alm.latency_background(f, mode, 1.0)
    near = f[np.abs(f - mode) <= 1.0]
    rows.append({"tag": tag, "unit": f"{s['session']}/{u['unit']}", "pulses": len(lat), "mode_ms": mode,
                 "obs_0.5": o05, "chance_0.5": e05, "obs_0.5_to_1": o10 - o05, "chance_0.5_to_1": e10 - e05,
                 "jitter_0.5": f[np.abs(f - mode) <= 0.5].std(ddof=1), "jitter_1": near.std(ddof=1),
                 "jitter_mad_1": 1.4826 * np.median(np.abs(near - np.median(near)))})
bg = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(bg[bg.tag == "IT"].round(3).to_string(index=False))
for tag, d in bg.groupby("tag"):
    print(f"\n{tag}: {len(d)} neurons; spikes 0.5 to 1 ms from the mode, observed {int(d['obs_0.5_to_1'].sum())}, expected by chance "
          f"{d['chance_0.5_to_1'].sum():.1f}; spikes within ±1 ms expected by chance as a fraction of those observed "
          f"{(d['chance_0.5_to_1'].sum() + d['chance_0.5'].sum()) / (d['obs_0.5'].sum() + d['obs_0.5_to_1'].sum()):.3f}")
    print(f"   mean jitter ±0.5 ms {d['jitter_0.5'].mean():.3f}, ±1 ms {d['jitter_1'].mean():.3f}, robust (MAD) {d['jitter_mad_1'].mean():.3f} ms")
print("\nTagged neurons, mean robust jitter:", round(bg.jitter_mad_1.mean(), 3), "ms;",
      "IT within 0.2 ± 0.05 ms:", bool(abs(bg[bg.tag == 'IT'].jitter_mad_1.mean() - 0.2) <= 0.05))
its = [(s, u) for s, u in units if "IT" in u["cell_types"]]
fig, axs = plt.subplots(4, 7, figsize=(16, 8)); axs = axs.ravel()
for ax, (s, u) in zip(axs, its):
    f = alm.antidromic_latencies(s, u, {2.0}, order=0)
    f = f[np.isfinite(f)]
    if len(f) >= 3:
        mode = alm.latency_mode(f)
        ax.hist(f, bins=np.arange(0, 10.01, 0.1), color="k")
        for hw, c in ((0.5, "tab:blue"), (1.0, "tab:red")):
            ax.axvline(mode - hw, color=c, lw=0.8); ax.axvline(mode + hw, color=c, lw=0.8)
    ax.set_title(f"{s['session'][3:]}/{u['unit']} n={len(f)}", fontsize=7); ax.tick_params(labelsize=6)
for ax in axs[len(its):]:
    ax.axis("off")
fig.suptitle("IT neurons, first-spike latency after the first pulse (ms; 0.1 ms bins), ±0.5 ms (blue) and ±1 ms (red) around the mode")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("Histograms span 0 to 10 ms, the whole latency window; IT neurons without type 2 responses are empty panels.")

# Readings without the window. (1) Per neuron, a maximum-likelihood fit to all first-spike
# latencies (0 to 10 ms) of a Gaussian peak plus a uniform background; (2) the same with a broad
# Gaussian (s.d. 1 to 5 ms) added to take up broad stimulus-locked humps; the jitter is the
# narrow peak's s.d. (3) The ±1 ms jitter without the four IT neurons whose histograms above show
# humps several ms wide (named in the round-2 verification).
rows = []
for s, u in units:
    tag = "PT" if "PT" in u["cell_types"] else "IT" if "IT" in u["cell_types"] else ""
    if not tag:
        continue
    lat = alm.antidromic_latencies(s, u, {1.0} if tag == "PT" else {2.0}, order=0)
    if np.isfinite(lat).sum() < 3:
        continue
    mu, sd, w, n = alm.latency_peak_fit(lat)
    mub, sdb, wb, _ = alm.latency_peak_fit(lat, broad=True)
    rows.append({"tag": tag, "unit": f"{s['session']}/{u['unit']}", "latencies": n, "peak_ms": mu, "jitter_fit": sd,
                 "peak_weight": w, "jitter_fit_broad": sdb, "peak_weight_broad": wb,
                 "jitter_1": alm.latency_mode_stats(lat, 1.0)[1], "jitter_0.5": alm.latency_mode_stats(lat, 0.5)[1]})
pf = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(pf[pf.tag == "IT"].round(3).to_string(index=False))
hump = ["ANM219253_20140122/4", "ANM219253_20140117/1", "ANM214427_20130808/2", "ANM219248_20130924/2"]
pf["broad_hump"] = pf.unit.isin(hump)
summ = []
for name, col, d in (("±1 ms window", "jitter_1", pf), ("±0.5 ms window", "jitter_0.5", pf),
                     ("peak + background fit", "jitter_fit", pf), ("peak + broad + background fit", "jitter_fit_broad", pf),
                     ("±1 ms, without the 4 broad-hump IT neurons", "jitter_1", pf[~pf.broad_hump])):
    summ.append({"reading": name, "PT_n": int((d.tag == "PT").sum()), "IT_n": int((d.tag == "IT").sum()),
                 "PT_jitter": d[d.tag == "PT"][col].mean(), "IT_jitter": d[d.tag == "IT"][col].mean(), "tagged_jitter": d[col].mean()})

±1 ms, without the 4 broad-hump IT neurons    45    17      0.126      0.289          0.170           True          False               False

Spikes of the 4 broad-hump neurons within 0.5 to 1 ms of the mode: 316 of 783 for all IT neurons

Result: partially reproduced, resting on the assumed ±1 ms window. With antidromic spikes taken within ±1 ms of each neuron's modal latency, first pulses, PT neurons have a mean latency of 2.672 ms and jitter 0.126 ms (45 neurons), within tolerance, and IT neurons 4.98 ms (21 neurons with type 2 trials; 4.56 ms with types 2 to 5, 27 neurons), within tolerance and longer than PT. The IT jitter is 0.310 ms (0.265 with types 2 to 5), outside 0.2 ± 0.05 ms, and the mean jitter of tagged neurons 0.184 ms (0.178), outside 0.15 ± 0.015 ms. Between 0.5 and 1 ms from the mode the IT neurons have 783 spikes where the spontaneous background predicts 69.7. This shows that those spikes are locked to the light pulse, not that they are antidromic: several IT histograms show humps several milliseconds wide, and the four neurons with the broadest humps hold 316 of the 783 spikes. The readings that need no window agree with ±1 ms: a fit of a peak plus background gives IT jitter 0.341 ms and a tagged mean of 0.185 ms, a fit with a broad component added 0.282 and 0.166 ms, and the ±1 ms window without the four broad-hump neurons 0.289 and 0.170 ms; the robust s.d. gives 0.289 and 0.166 ms. Only the ±0.5 ms window gives values that match the paper (IT 0.198 ms, 0.177 with types 2 to 5; tagged mean 0.140 ms). The PT values (jitter 0.112 to 0.126 ms), the latencies and their order hold under every reading; the IT jitter and the tagged mean hold only under the ±0.5 ms window. The activated neurons are not labelled, so their values cannot be computed.

ed5g-it-second-pulse-jitter¶

After a conditioning pulse, IT neurons respond to a second light pulse 10 ms later with less temporal jitter.

Result: reproduced. In every variant the mean jitter of IT neurons is lower for the second pulse than for the first (0.156 against 0.204 ms with type 2 trials and ±0.5 ms; 0.232 against 0.280 ms with types 2 to 5 and ±1 ms), and 65% to 87% of IT neurons show the decrease (Wilcoxon p 0.004 to 0.098). 4 to 8 IT neurons with fewer than three responses to either pulse are left out.

Result: reproduced, under the reading of selective neurons. Among selective neurons (reading b, lick early dropped, 1.3 s response) 24 of 38 PT neurons prefer contra (0.632, P = 0.033) and 10 of 23 IT neurons (0.435, P = 0.74, the paper's value). With lick early trials kept the PT P is 0.017 (1.3 s) and 0.037 (1.5 s); with a 1.5 s response epoch and lick early dropped it is 0.068. Among all tagged neurons (reading a) PT is not significant under any reading (0.556 to 0.600, P = 0.089 to 0.23) while IT stays far from it (P = 0.58 to 0.72). Keeping only the selective neurons with more than 15 correct trials of each type (reading c, not one of the criterion's readings) PT is not significant either: 19 of 32 contra-preferring (0.594, P = 0.11) with lick early dropped and a 1.3 s response epoch, P = 0.054 to 0.20 over the four readings. The data set's IT_PT script applies that filter to the curve of all selective pyramidal neurons in Fig. 3f (line 25), and takes the PT and IT fractions from the selective neurons with no trial filter (lines 170 and 195, printed above). The outcome depends on which neurons enter, which the paper does not say.

fig3f-late-contra-selectivity-pt¶

Robust contralateral selectivity emerges in PT neurons starting 570 ms before the response epoch (34% spike rate modulation, P < 0.05), but not in IT neurons (-19%, P = 0.40) nor in all task-selective neurons (8%, P = 0.13).

Contra-selectivity is R minus L rate per neuron (correct trials, 200 ms windows, 10 ms step). Onset readings (a) the earliest window centre from which the PT mean stays significantly above 0 (t-test across neurons, P < 0.05) through the window centred 0.1 s before the cue, (b) the first significant window after sample onset. Modulation windows (a) 570 ms before the cue to the cue, (b) to the end of the response epoch; percentage of (a) the mean rate over both trial types in the window, (b) the mean rate in the 0.5 s before sample onset. Neurons (a) all PT (IT), (b) the selective ones; "all task-selective" is the selective pyramidal neurons. Every combination is run under the four readings of the shared methods (lick early trials dropped or kept, response epoch 1.3 or 1.5 s), with the selective neurons taken under the same reading.

In [27]:
def cs_curve(keys, le="drop"):
    out = []
    for s, u in units:
        if (s["session"], u["unit"]) not in keys:
            continue
        tr = s["trials"]
        r, l = alm.trial_mask(tr, u, lick_early=le)
        if r.sum() < 2 or l.sum() < 2:
            continue
        out.append((alm.window_sums(alm.cue_binned(u, tr, r))[0].mean(axis=0) - alm.window_sums(alm.cue_binned(u, tr, l))[0].mean(axis=0)) / alm.WIN_S)
    return np.array(out)

def win_rates(keys, a_rel, b_rel, le="drop"):
    rows = []
    for s, u in units:
        if (s["session"], u["unit"]) not in keys:
            continue
        tr = s["trials"]
        r, l = alm.trial_mask(tr, u, lick_early=le)
        if r.sum() < 2 or l.sum() < 2:
            continue
        a, b = tr.cue.values + a_rel, tr.cue.values + b_rel
        pa, pb_ = tr.pole_in.values - 0.5, tr.pole_in.values
        R = alm.counts_in(u, tr, r, a, b).mean() / (b_rel - a_rel)
        L = alm.counts_in(u, tr, l, a, b).mean() / (b_rel - a_rel)
        base = (alm.counts_in(u, tr, r, pa, pb_).mean() + alm.counts_in(u, tr, l, pa, pb_).mean()) / 2 / 0.5
        rows.append((R, L, base))
    return np.array(rows)

keyset = lambda d: set(map(tuple, d[["session", "unit"]].values))

def fig3f(le, resp):
    d = UT[(le, resp)]
    groups = {"PT a all": keyset(d[d.tag == "PT"]), "PT b selective": keyset(d[(d.tag == "PT") & d.selective]),
              "IT a all": keyset(d[d.tag == "IT"]), "IT b selective": keyset(d[(d.tag == "IT") & d.selective]),
              "all task-selective": keyset(d[(d.label == "pyramidal") & d.selective])}
    onsets = []
    for name in ("PT a all", "PT b selective"):
        C = cs_curve(groups[name], le)
        p = stats.ttest_1samp(C, 0, axis=0).pvalue
        sigpos = (p < 0.05) & (C.mean(axis=0) > 0)
        idx = np.flatnonzero((centers >= t_sample) & (centers <= -0.1))
        stay = None
        for i in idx[::-1]:
            if sigpos[i]:
                stay = centers[i]
            else:
                break
        first = centers[idx][sigpos[idx]][0] if sigpos[idx].any() else np.nan
        onsets.append({"lick_early": le, "response_s": resp, "neurons": name, "n": len(C),
                       "onset_a_stays_ms_before_cue": -1e3 * stay if stay is not None else np.nan,
                       "onset_b_first_ms_before_cue": -1e3 * first})
    rows = []
    for wname, (a_rel, b_rel) in (("a -0.57 to cue", (-0.57, 0.0)), ("b -0.57 to response end", (-0.57, resp))):
        for name, keys in groups.items():
            X = win_rates(keys, a_rel, b_rel, le)
            dlt = X[:, 0] - X[:, 1]
            rows.append({"lick_early": le, "response_s": resp, "window": wname, "neurons": name, "n": len(X),
                         "mean_R_minus_L": dlt.mean(), "p": stats.ttest_1samp(dlt, 0).pvalue,
                         "mod_pct_a_window_rate": 100 * dlt.mean() / ((X[:, 0] + X[:, 1]) / 2).mean(),
                         "mod_pct_b_baseline": 100 * dlt.mean() / X[:, 2].mean()})
    return pd.DataFrame(onsets), pd.DataFrame(rows)

Combinations with the paper's pattern of significance: 0 of 32 ; with the pattern and all values within tolerance: 0
All task-selective neurons, window a: P under the four readings: [{'lick_early': 'drop', 'response_s': 1.3, 'n': 912, 'p': 0.024}, {'lick_early': 'drop', 'response_s': 1.5, 'n': 910, 'p': 0.0229}, {'lick_early': 'keep', 'response_s': 1.3, 'n': 950, 'p': 0.0231}, {'lick_early': 'keep', 'response_s': 1.5, 'n': 948, 'p': 0.0221}]

Result: not reproduced. Over the 570 ms before the cue, the PT spike rate modulation is 34.4% of the window rate (P = 0.027), the paper's value, and the IT modulation -16.4% (P = 0.11, not significant; the paper has -19%). But all task-selective neurons show 9.2% (P = 0.024), significant where the paper has 8% with P = 0.13, so the pattern of significance does not hold in this window. Over the window to the end of the response epoch, all task-selective neurons are not significant (0.18%, P = 0.96) but neither is PT (20.6%, P = 0.068). The four readings of the shared methods change none of this: all task-selective neurons give P = 0.022 to 0.024 in the pre-cue window, PT gives P = 0.068 to 0.114 in the longer window, and none of the 32 combinations has the paper's pattern of significance. The PT contra-selectivity stays significant only from 190 to 310 ms before the cue (onset reading a) and is first significant 2,470 to 2,490 ms before it (reading b), against the paper's 570 ms.

reaction-time¶

The reaction time after go cue onset is 61.1 +/- 10.5 ms across mice (mean +/- s.d.).

First movement of the lick trace after the cue. The paper gives no detection rule; two rules are run (helper docstring). The noise rule takes the first sample from which the trace stays, for 5 ms, further from its pre-cue baseline than k times the baseline noise and at least a floor (k = 3, 5, 10; floor 2 or 5 mV). The peak rule takes the first sample at which the trace has moved by a fraction (5% to 50%) of its largest excursion in the 1 s after the cue. Trials (a) correct trials without early licks, (b) all performing trials with a response (hit or error); both only trials of type 0, without axonal stimulation or the NaN-type test stimulation. Per mouse the mean, then mean and s.d. across mice; per-mouse medians are a variant. Example traces with the onsets marked, and per-mouse histograms of the onsets, follow the table.

Onsets beyond 400 ms (not shown): noise rule 54 ; peak rule 192 of 12639 trials

Result: blocked, methods underspecified. The paper does not say how the first mouth movement is found in the photodiode trace, and the outcome turns on that choice. On correct trials, the noise rule gives a mean over the 19 mice of 65.0 ms (s.d. 21.1) at 3 times the noise with a 2 mV floor, within 61.1 ± 10.5 ms, 71.7 ms with a 5 mV floor, just outside, and 77.7 to 103.7 ms at 5 and 10 times the noise; on all responses 3 times the noise gives 65.0 and 71.3 ms, both within. The peak rule gives 81.7 to 176.8 ms (s.d. 57 to 65 ms), with per-mouse means from 16 to 320 ms. Neither threshold has a better basis: before the cue the noise rule fires within 0.1 s in 11.6% to 16.0% of trials at 3 times the noise and 6.5% to 8.2% at 5 times, so the lower threshold is more sensitive to the first movement and more prone to early triggers. The spread across mice is 21 to 36 ms under the noise rule, two to three times the paper's 10.5 ms, which also points to a different procedure or set of mice. Per-session means under the noise rule (5 times the noise, 5 mV) range from 34 to 212 ms; the example traces show sessions where the trace is a two-level signal or carries brief cue-locked deflections.

contra-ipsi-selectivity-forms¶

Contra-preferring neurons include most of the neurons with large spike count differences between trial types, while ipsi-preferring neurons more often express their selectivity through suppression of activity on contra trials.

Per selective pyramidal neuron, the absolute difference of R and L rates from sample onset to the end of the response epoch. Contra-suppression: the rate on R trials (same span) below the rate in the 0.5 s before sample onset, with the rate on L trials not below it; ipsi-suppression is the same with the trial types swapped. The whole pre-sample period is a variant baseline.

In [30]:
sp = pyr[pyr.selective].copy()
sp["absdiff"] = (sp.trial_R - sp.trial_L).abs()
rows = []
for q, name in ((0.75, "a top quarter"), (0.90, "b top tenth")):
    big = sp[sp.absdiff >= sp.absdiff.quantile(q)]
    rows.append({"reading": name, "neurons": len(big), "fraction_contra": big.contra.mean(), "binomial_p": stats.binomtest(int(big.contra.sum()), len(big)).pvalue})
large = pd.DataFrame(rows)
large["contra_majority"] = large.fraction_contra > 0.5
print(large.round(4).to_string(index=False))
rows = []
for bname, bcol in (("0.5 s pre-sample", "pre"), ("whole pre-sample (variant)", "pre_all")):
    base = (sp[f"{bcol}_R"] + sp[f"{bcol}_L"]) / 2
    csup = (sp.trial_R < base) & ~(sp.trial_L < base)
    isup = (sp.trial_L < base) & ~(sp.trial_R < base)
    ip, cp = sp[~sp.contra], sp[sp.contra]
    rows.append({"baseline": bname, "ipsi_pref_n": len(ip), "ipsi_pref_with_contra_suppression": float(csup[~sp.contra].mean()),
                 "contra_pref_n": len(cp), "contra_pref_with_ipsi_suppression": float(isup[sp.contra].mean()),
                 "fisher_p": stats.fisher_exact([[int(csup[~sp.contra].sum()), len(ip) - int(csup[~sp.contra].sum())],
                                                 [int(isup[sp.contra].sum()), len(cp) - int(isup[sp.contra].sum())]])[1]})
sup = pd.DataFrame(rows)
sup["ipsi_more"] = sup.ipsi_pref_with_contra_suppression > sup.contra_pref_with_ipsi_suppression
print(sup.round(4).to_string(index=False))

Result: partially reproduced. Contra-preferring neurons are a slight majority of the neurons with the largest rate differences (0.535 of the top quarter, 228 neurons, binomial p = 0.32; 0.522 of the top tenth, p = 0.75). Contra-suppression in ipsi-preferring neurons (0.365) is not more common than ipsi-suppression in contra-preferring neurons (0.389, Fisher p = 0.49); the whole pre-sample baseline gives the same (0.367 against 0.391). The four readings of the shared methods give the same: contra fractions 0.522 to 0.558 of the large groups, contra-suppression 0.360 to 0.388 against ipsi-suppression 0.389 to 0.418. The first part holds weakly and the second does not.

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. Only the 19 electrophysiology mice are in the data set, so task performance and reaction time are measured on them alone. Where the paper leaves a detail open, the data set's own MATLAB scripts were followed and the choice is stated: the response epoch of 1.3 s, the exclusion of lick early and axonal stimulation trials, each unit's trials limited to its recorded span, preference from the counts from sample onset to the end of the response epoch. The paper gives no rule for telling antidromic from spontaneous spikes; the ±1 ms window is an assumption, and readings without a window (fits of a peak plus background) agree with it, while only a ±0.5 ms window gives the paper's IT jitter. Nor does it give a rule for detecting the first mouth movement in the lick trace; on correct trials the reaction time is within tolerance only at 3 times the noise with a 2 mV floor and outside it under every other rule, so that claim is blocked as underspecified. Spike widths are recomputed from the deposited 29-sample waveforms.

What was found about the data set. The electrophysiology matches the paper closely: 1,408 units, 19 mice, 99 sessions, the labels' 1,245 pyramidal, 124 FS, 45 PT and 27 IT neurons, and the paper's 912 selective neurons, response categories and contra and ipsi counts are recovered exactly. The data set's description lists photostimulation types 0, 1, 2 and NaN; types 3, 4 and 5 also occur (IT tagging in the Tlx x Ai32 mice). 43 trials of type 0 in session ANM210862_20130627 carry light pulses. The trough-to-peak widths of the deposited waveforms put 34 of the 39 unlabelled units below 0.35 ms, so the "intermediate" class cannot be recomputed with the stated thresholds; the labels split the deposited widths at 0.256 to 0.307 ms and 0.410 to 0.461 ms. The activated (non-collision) neurons are not labelled. The lick trace differs in baseline, scale and sign between sessions and is not described beyond "licking movement from photodiode". The NaN-type test trials carry light in all 19 mice, at onsets and powers the description does not give. 10 units have spike times out of order. The NWB copies omit the photostimulation type, the AOM and laser traces and GoodTrials. The behaviour, imaging and anatomy of Figs 1, 4 and 5 and ED Figs 3, 6 and 7 are not in the data set.
